issues.legal_issue: A dispute seeking enforcement of rights under an accession or merger agreement is outside the courts’ jurisdiction when it arises from that agreement.
material_facts: The former ruler relied on the Instrument of Accession and Merger Agreement to argue that the land-acquisition law could not affect his rights.
The dispute concerned the effect of those agreements on his rights after the state had been ceded and integrated.
issues.conclusion: The courts could not inquire into the dispute arising from the agreements.
issues.legal_principle: Article 363(1) of the Constitution bars judicial inquiry into disputes arising out of specified agreements and covenants relating to the integration of Indian States. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.constitutional_property_challenge: A person brings a constitutional challenge concerning the effect of a land measure on claimed property rights.
predicates.claim_based_on_state_integration_agreeme: The person bases the claimed property protection on an agreement made in connection with the integration of a former state.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property challenge rests on a state-integration agreement, the court cannot adjudicate the agreement dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A person who surrendered the governance of a former state is an ex-ruler for purposes outside the Constitution, even if constitutionally recognized as a ruler for specified constitutional purposes.
material_facts: The ruler ceded the state and transferred full and exclusive authority over its governance to the Government of India.
The President recognized him as a ruler under the Constitution, which provided for the privy purse.
The land-acquisition law expressly included an ex-ruler of a merged Indian State within its definition of proprietor.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was an ex-ruler for purposes of the Act and fell within the class of persons included in the definition of proprietor.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 291 and 366(22) of the Constitution concern the privy purse and the constitutional meaning of ruler; they do not require constitutional recognition as a ruler to apply outside the Constitution. Section 2(m) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, expressly included an ex-ruler of a merged Indian State. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.land_rights_challenged_under_abolition_s: A person challenges the application of a land-rights abolition measure to land claimed by that person.
predicates.former_ruler_surrendered_state_governanc: A former ruler transferred the state’s governance and authority to another government.
predicates.constitutional_ruler_recognition_for_lim: A former ruler continued to be recognized as a ruler for specified constitutional purposes.
predicates.law_includes_former_rulers_as_proprietor: The applicable law expressly includes former rulers among the persons treated as proprietors.

issues.definition: If a person challenges an abolition measure, surrendered state governance, remains constitutionally recognized only for limited purposes, and the law includes former rulers as proprietors, that person falls within the proprietor class.

issues.legal_issue: A holder of land exempt from rent or tax may be a maufidar even without being a grantee from a state or ruler.
material_facts: The villages in question were exempt from payment of rent or tax.
The appellant held the land but argued that a maufidar had to be a grantee from a state or ruler.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was a maufidar because the term also covered a holder of land exempt from rent or tax.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(m) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, used maufidar in a sense that was not confined to a grantee; the ordinary meaning included a holder of rent-free land. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.property_abolition_classification_disput: A dispute concerns whether a person falls within a land-rights classification used by an abolition measure.
predicates.person_holds_land_exempt_from_rent_or_ta: A person holds land that is exempt from payment of rent or tax.

issues.definition: In a property-classification dispute, a person who holds land exempt from rent or tax qualifies as a maufidar.

issues.legal_issue: A maufidar’s inclusion as a proprietor depends on the applicable village record providing for a right to recover rent or revenue, but a claimant who fails to prove the absence of that right cannot rely on its absence.
material_facts: The statutory definition connected a maufidar’s status as proprietor to a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in the village, as provided in the applicable village record.
The appellant first argued on appeal that the village records did not provide such a right.
The appellant had not raised or supported that contention with evidence in the lower court or the appellate record.
issues.conclusion: The contention was rejected because the appellant had the burden of proving the absence of the right and had not discharged it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(m) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, required the specified right to recover rent or revenue in the case of a maufidar. The claimant bore the burden of establishing the asserted absence of that right. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_in_property_abolition_dispute: A person appeals in a dispute over whether land or its holder falls within a property-abolition classification.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_absence_of_collection: The claimant argues that the applicable village record does not provide a right to recover rent or revenue from landholders.
predicates.claimant_provides_no_evidence_of_absence: The claimant supplies no evidence establishing that the village record lacks the asserted right.

issues.definition: In an appeal over a property-abolition classification, a claimant who relies on the absence of a collection right but provides no evidence of that absence has that contention rejected.

issues.legal_issue: Land falls within the statutory definition of a mahal only if it has been separately assessed to land revenue, and a claimant who fails to establish that it was not assessed cannot defeat its classification on that ground.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the villages had not been assessed to land revenue, while the State disputed that claim.
The appellant produced no evidence establishing that the villages had never been assessed.
Documents showed that at least the Bhandar villages had been assessed to land revenue.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s contention that the villages were not mahals because they had not been assessed to land revenue was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(j) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, defined a mahal in the merged territories by reference to land separately assessed to land revenue. The claimant bore the burden of establishing the factual assertion that the land had not been assessed. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_in_land_classification_dispute: A person appeals a decision classifying land under a land-rights measure.
predicates.claimant_says_land_was_not_assessed: The claimant asserts that the land was not separately assessed to land revenue.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_prove_nonassessment: The claimant presents no sufficient evidence that the land was never assessed.

issues.definition: In a land-classification appeal, a claimant who asserts nonassessment but fails to prove it has that contention rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional petition asserting ownership over property not recognized as the claimant’s private property by the government is not maintainable on that basis.
material_facts: The appellant asserted ownership over villages that had not been recognized by the Government of India as his private property.
The claimed ownership depended on the Merger Agreement’s provisions concerning recognition of private property.
issues.conclusion: The petition was not maintainable as to those villages because they had not been recognized as the appellant’s private property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the relevant provisions of the Merger Agreement concerning recognition of private property and held that Article 363(1) barred judicial inquiry into disputes arising from that agreement. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.constitutional_property_petition: A person brings a constitutional petition asserting ownership of particular property.
predicates.ownership_claim_depends_on_government_re: The asserted ownership depends on the government having recognized the property as the claimant’s private property.
predicates.property_not_recognized_as_claimant_priv: The government has not recognized the property as the claimant’s private property.

issues.definition: A constitutional petition is not maintainable as to property when the ownership claim depends on government recognition and that recognition has not occurred.
